findings: 26.0% of all city-days fall in the Poor, Very Poor or Severe AQI categories, while only 5.4% are rated Good.

Ahmedabad has the highest mean AQI (452.1) among the 19 cities with at least a year of data, while Thiruvananthapuram has the lowest (75.9). Ahmedabad has the largest share of Poor-or-worse days (81.9%).
Pollution varies with the season: mean PM2.5 is highest in Winter and lowest in Monsoon, a 2.58x difference. The worst month on average is November and the best is August.
The seasonal difference is statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis H = 6423.9, p < 0.001).
AQI is most strongly correlated with PM10 (r = 0.8), followed by CO (r = 0.68) and PM2.5 (r = 0.66).
PM2.5 and PM10 move together (Spearman rho = 0.873), and the median PM2.5 reading is about 47% of the PM10 reading on the same day.
Average PM2.5 across cities was 75.1 µg/m³ in 2015 and 43.7 µg/m³ in 2020 (the final year is partial). The number of reporting cities changes over the years, so this trend should be read cautiously.

In the COVID-19 lockdown window (25 Mar - 30 Apr), mean PM2.5 fell by 38.3% compared with the same dates in 2019 (55.0 to 33.9 µg/m³; 17 of 19 cities improved). A Wilcoxon signed-rank test on city means shows this is significant (p < 0.001).
A random forest predicts next-day PM2.5 with R² = 0.726 and MAE = 9.57 µg/m³ on unseen later dates, compared with R² = 0.742 and MAE = 8.81 for the simple 'tomorrow equals today' baseline.
conclusion: Winter has the highest PM2.5 levels and Monsoon the lowest, a 2.58x difference (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.001). 26.0% of recorded city-days were Poor or worse, and Ahmedabad was the most polluted city on average (mean AQI 452.1). AQI follows particulate matter most closely.
The prediction model did not beat the simple 'tomorrow equals today' baseline, which suggests day-to-day PM2.5 is mostly explained by today's PM2.5 alone.

Limitations: the dataset has many missing values (only short gaps were filled), monitoring stations differ between cities and years, and the analysis shows association, not cause. Weather data such as wind and rainfall would improve both the analysis and the model.
